Warsh, Opening Remarks
headlines.officialText: The Nobel laureate Paul Romer, among others, has shown that a doubling of ideas and other key inputs can more than double output, allowing increasing returns to scale.1 Even so, in the U.S. The conventional view holds that as population growth slows, there may be fewer new ideas to drive prosperity.3 The increasing challenge of generating breakthrough ideas, combined with slower population growth, helps explain why many in the economics profession, in the post-crisis environment, returned to the theme of secular stagnation. And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly. Our responsibility is to recognize that the widespread adoption of this technology will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road. An SI-driven expansion could bring substantial labor market disruption as some jobs are displaced, rather than complemented, by technology. But widespread automation, combined with labor market frictions, could push the jobless rate above levels consistent with full employment. After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment.

Barr, Some Potential Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
headlines.officialText: One of the reasons I'm optimistic about this technology is that I'm also optimistic about the capacity of society to understand and respond to the changes that AI will bring—to engage in a constructive dialogue about ensuring that the benefits from AI are not overwhelmed by the disruptions it will inevitably bring and the risks it may pose. I will recap the report's findings and then turn to a discussion of what economic research can tell us about the benefits and risks of integrating AI into financial markets, focusing on wholesale trading. Next, I will examine the potential benefits and risks of AI's effect on cybersecurity and then finally consider what AI might mean for consumer and investor protection. Leverage in the Data Center Buildout In addition to the question of equity valuations, the AI buildout has been increasingly funded by debt. These investments represent a relatively small share of the hyperscalers' and GPU producers' balance sheets, but they are critical for the smaller firms receiving the investments. As with any new technology, however, there are risks. While it is my understanding that generative AI is not yet being used for autonomous trading at large scale, we need to be prepared to understand the risks and implications of its adoption.8 Many of the most important questions about how AI will affect financial markets will be answered not in the abstract, but in the technical choices made about model design, training data, testing, and deployment. While AI can democratize access to trading expertise and technology, it could also increase information asymmetry and market concentration.9 The state-of-the art systems are expensive and require massive investment.10 This could confer an advantage on the largest firms and concentrate market power among them.11 Even when AI tools are widely available, effectively using them requires considerable skill, potentially favoring larger incumbents.12 The implications for price efficiency of the integration of AI into financial market trading are ambiguous.13 In his 2026 Jackson Hole paper, Markus Brunnermeier cautioned that securities prices may also become less informative because of asymmetric understanding: AI agents understand humans and can anticipate their actions, but humans do not understand AI agents as well and cannot anticipate what they might do.14 Market Herding and a Possible Stampede If traders rely on a small set of similar AI models trained on similar data, they face the risk of herding behavior—trading strategies could become similar and synchronize reactions to news and other information.15 Algorithm flaws can cause failures, but a market with large numbers of similar models that may have the same flaw risks failures with systemic consequences.16 Moreover, bad actors could intentionally manipulate trades, quotes, or news and potentially mislead similar AI trading systems at the same time, amplifying market disruptions.17 AI models may echo unfortunate human tendencies. For example, some theoretical research shows that some reinforcement-learning algorithms, so called Q-learning trading algorithms, can autonomously develop collusive behavior without explicit intent.18 Such self-learning algorithms can also autonomously learn to manipulate markets—for example, through spoofing, which is placing orders designed to create a false impression of market demand—or adopt trading strategies that create and exploit bubbles, thereby destabilizing markets.19 To attempt to combat such potential risks, exchanges are deploying sophisticated machine learning and AI tools themselves for market surveillance.20 Some trading venues are already acting to reduce risks from the "black box" nature of AI-enabled trading algorithms.21 Since we all have an interest in safe, fair, and efficient markets, we need to think through the risks and implications before any new technology is integrated into trading activity or market infrastructure more broadly. AI and Cyber Risk Incidents this year have shown the risks from AI models acting autonomously, not in alignment with the goals of their human creators, including cyber risks. I have spoken before, for example, about how AI can raise cyber risks through its use in creating deepfakes.22 Just like the attackers, cyber defenders are employing AI, finding and patching vulnerabilities much faster than humans ever could.

Jefferson, New Technology, Old Questions: Productivity Puzzles and the Macroeconomy
headlines.officialText: The topics I want to focus on today are relevant for all of us: How could rapid technological change affect our economy, and what could that mean for monetary policy? Then, I will consider the implications of rapid technological change for the economy more broadly, including for aggregate supply and demand, for inflation, and for the labor market. Finally, I will discuss briefly my thinking about the economic outlook and monetary policy. While 32 percent of workers used computers at work in 1989, the computers were not very powerful. Over time, firms intensify their use of lower-priced capital goods produced by higher productivity, a process known as "capital deepening." Finally, firms using that capital rethink their approach to production, further increasing TFP and, perhaps, starting the investment cycle again. Labor productivity growth averaged 2.2 percent between 2020 and 2025, a welcome step up from the modest 1.5 percent average growth rate seen over the previous business cycle. Teasing out the contribution of AI to recent productivity growth is not straightforward. For example, one recent study surveyed senior managers and estimated that AI has boosted sales per employee by just 1/2 percent over the past three years.16 What could explain this apparent disconnect between task-level and firm-level gains? Implications for the Macroeconomy What does all this mean for my thinking about macroeconomic activity? Expectations of those longer-term gains on the supply side of the economy are already increasing aggregate demand significantly. One risk to my baseline outlook is that the new technology could displace workers much faster than they can adapt and retrain, which could result in an increase in unemployment. In this scenario, a key question for monetary policy would be how much of this increase is structural—reflecting a persistent mismatch between worker skills and firms' needs—and therefore likely to persist even when the economy is operating close to its full potential. Monetary policy can affect cyclical conditions, like a temporary downturn in employment and spending, but it cannot address the structural factors that determine long-run rates of employment. As a monetary policymaker, I must also consider the potential effects of the new technology on the longer-run neutral rate of interest, often called r*. If the neutral rate rises, then for any given level of the federal funds rate, policy effectively becomes more accommodative. Conversely, if the neutral rate declines, then policy effectively becomes more restrictive. If the new technology leads to permanently higher levels of productivity growth, it may increase firms' desire to invest and, hence, their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates. As I discussed earlier, higher productivity growth may also discourage household savings and raise consumption by increasing expected future income. However, predicting changes in the neutral rate of interest is challenging, given the historically noisy relationship between productivity growth and real interest rates. Policymakers must remain attentive to real-time developments and potential future developments to ensure that the stance of monetary policy remains appropriately calibrated.

headlines.title: Barr, American Inequality and the Future of AI
headlines.officialText: Inequality is an aspect of every economy, and understanding the extent and evolution of inequality in the United States can help in forming a clear view of the economic outlook and how the economy is likely to react to new developments. By contrast, the entire lower half of households, as measured by wealth holdings, have only 2 percent of wealth. Private equity investments are 12 percent of the assets of the wealthiest 0.1 percent of households in the most recent Fed survey. The group of households in the 50th through the 90th percentiles of wealth hold only 17 percent of all public stocks by value, underscoring how much wealth is concentrated.8 Finally, on net, households in the bottom half of the wealth distribution hold just over 2 percent of all wealth, an average of $52,000. This was a period of slower economic growth and sometimes high inflation. Moreover, minimum wage laws failed to keep up with inflation and the growth of the economy.13 The lesson from this history is that the level of inequality in American society is not immutable—it changes over time. Technology replacing labor has been going on for centuries, but new technology can also augment the productivity of existing jobs and create new jobs, including those that are hard to envision when the technology is initially adopted, a point I have noted in a number of speeches.17 The internet and the businesses it created reduced employment in some occupations—such as travel agents—and eliminated others: Think video store workers. AI could be what some researchers call capital-biased innovation, in which the returns go primarily to capital rather than to labor.26 In previous remarks, I have explored scenarios for how AI could evolve as a technology and how it could affect labor markets. The nature of AI, particularly its ability to learn how to complete complex, nonroutine tasks that require extensive knowledge difficult for humans to achieve, raises the question of whether AI's effects on the labor market will be stronger than other technologies. So far, there has been relatively little displacement of workers by AI and some significant evidence that the transition to AI is enhancing the productivity of some workers, increasing demand in some sectors, and even creating new occupations. Some tasks that are easily automated with clear guardrails and predictable outcomes might see rapid labor substitution, while other tasks that require human judgment, management, coordination and relationships, creativity, or outputs that are hard to measure might see more labor augmentation.30 If labor market changes happen quickly, it will be hard for workers to adjust, and dislocations might be large, whereas a more gradual adoption might permit more orderly adjustments. That said, we should be prepared for the possibility of serious short-term disruptions in the labor market that need to be managed effectively to ensure the benefits of AI are realized over the long term. If AI proves to be capable of work that displaces humans, the extent of the disruption to the labor market will depend in part on whether society undertakes the investments needed in new job creation and worker training, connecting workers to new jobs, and other efforts to mitigate adverse effects for the long term. The sources of income collected in the survey include wages, self-employment and business income, taxable and tax-exempt interest, dividends, realized capital gains, unemployment insurance, food stamps and other related support programs provided by the government, pensions and withdrawals from retirement accounts, Social Security, alimony and other support payments, and miscellaneous sources. Bowman, The U.S. Economy and Considerations for Monetary Policy
headlines.officialText: economy.1 Economic growth has gained momentum this year, driven by robust investment demand and solid consumer spending, and the labor market now appears to have stabilized. These outcomes suggest that the policy rate cuts toward the end of last year helped to address some labor market weakness. We are experiencing rapid technological change and ongoing geopolitical tensions, while inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped and have shown recent signs of broadening. The Federal Reserve's monetary policy goals are to achieve maximum employment and price stability. While the labor market has improved more than I expected this year, our progress on lowering inflation has disappointed. Therefore, bringing inflation down remains a priority. I am also monitoring expectations about AI and energy prices, and how they influence the risks to achieving our mandates. I will then turn to recent developments in energy markets and the AI buildout and will conclude with my thoughts on the appropriate path of monetary policy. Update on the Most Recent FOMC Meeting At last month's FOMC meeting, I joined my colleagues to support holding the federal funds rate target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent. This approach was consistent with my view that further changes in the policy rate should wait until we had a better understanding of how conditions would evolve and how the recent rate increase would influence the underlying trends in the economy. While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated. After rising a solid 2.4 percent during the first half of the year, real gross domestic product (GDP) likely increased at an even stronger pace of more than 3 percent in the third quarter, well above last year's 2 percent pace.3 Economic growth has been supported by robust increases in AI-related capital expenditures and solid consumer spending. Labor Market Conditions Labor market conditions look to have improved since last year. Over the course of this year, the unemployment rate has edged down to 4.1 percent in October, remaining close to my estimate of its natural rate. The labor market continues to show low dynamism, with low-hiring and low-firing conditions as we sometimes see in a late-cycle expansion. On their own, these data would be consistent with a higher unemployment rate than currently reported. Although stable, the labor market does not appear to be tight, as wage growth has slowed to a modest pace. On a 12-month basis, the wages and salaries component of the employment cost index increased 3.1 percent in September, the same pace as the change in average hourly earnings for October. An increasing number of workers have taken on a supplemental part-time job to make ends meet, as the share of multiple job holders has increased back to levels seen in early 2025. Given strong productivity gains in recent years, wage growth at this pace is in line with or even below the pace we would expect if inflation was running at 2 percent.
